extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and general readers interested in the philosophy/sociology of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A literary/philosophical sketch of the 'ideal mathematician' that articulates beliefs, communicative conventions, and standards about proofs, existence, publication, and the social life of mathematics. Useful for understanding implicit criteria that govern mathematical practice and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: He rests his faith on rigorous proof; he believes that the difference between a correct proof and an incorrect one is an unmistakable and decisive difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes the ideal mathematician's conviction that rigor is decisive, but also notes his inability to give a coherent explanation of what 'rigor' requires and that the line between complete and incomplete proof is 'always somewhat fuzzy, and often controversial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-definition view of proof (logicist account)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a formal derivation: write down the axioms in a formal language, write the hypothesis, and transform hypothesis step by step using rules of logic until the conclusion is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the logician/Tarski-style definition. The text immediately qualifies it: 'Of course no one ever really does it. It would take forever! You just show that you could do it, that's sufficient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as convincing someone knowledgeable
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is 'an argument that convinces someone who knows the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational/communicative definition makes proof dependent on the intended audience's background and implies an apprenticeship: conviction is relative to the experts who judge the argument; hence proof standards have a social/subjective element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence as model-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying that mathematical objects 'exist' means that 'the axioms for a hypersquare possess a model' — i.e., 'no formal contradiction can be deduced from them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames 'existence' in formal/model-theoretic terms: existence = consistency (the axioms have a model), which is presented as the mathematician's practical usage rather than a metaphysical claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and reputation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: He is labeled by his field, by how much he publishes, and especially by whose work he uses, and by whose taste he follows in his choice of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes social criteria for evaluating mathematicians: quantity of publication, intellectual lineage (whose work one uses), and whose taste one follows informally determine reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success measured by discovering new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: His life is successful to the extent that he can discover new facts about [his objects].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success is defined internally by contribution to knowledge about the subject (new theorems/results), not by external application or public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem prestige depends on origin and partial solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem is important because 'Professor Nameless stated it and gave a partial solution... Since Professor Nameless' day, all the best ... have worked on the problem, obtaining many partial results. Thus the problem has acquired great prestige.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige of problems arises historically (who posed it) and sociologically (who works on it and the partial results), not solely from intrinsic applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tier communication: casual oral shorthand vs dense published formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: At conferences the mathematician uses a 'breezy style' and casual shorthand; published writings 'pile up formalism on top of formalism' with lengthy definitions and lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry highlights that mathematical production involves an informal communicative mode for insiders and a formalized published mode that conceals the informal motivations and makes the work accessible only to initiated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing convention: conceal the human author and reader
rubrics_metrics.description: His writing follows an unbreakable convention: to conceal any sign that the author or the intended reader is a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: papers present apparently mechanical deductions from definitions, masking the background knowledge, motivations, and standard arguments that insiders use to 'decode' the new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of apprenticeship and shared subculture for comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to go through an arduous apprenticeship of several years to understand the theory; the intended readers (all twelve of them) can decode the formal presentation because they share motivations, standard arguments and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding requires immersion in a subculture of motivations, examples, and agreed-upon modes of reasoning; otherwise the formal presentation remains a cipher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community role in proof validation and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: He has twice convinced himself he had solved the decision problem, but gaps were discovered by other devotees and the problem remains open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that validation is communal: peer scrutiny discovers gaps; progress and acceptance depend on other experts' evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reluctance to translate work for outsiders or to seek publicity at cost of integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't want the public to sympathize if it means 'debasing myself' by getting involved in public relations gimmicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal mathematician resists simplifying or sensationalizing work for popular consumption if that would compromise perceived intellectual integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited concern for applications or public intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked about applications or understandability by ordinary citizens, the mathematician replies 'No' or 'I doubt it very much.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures a value judgment: pure mathematical work may be judged internally valuable despite lacking evident applications or broad comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational approach to understanding mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the meaning of 'exist' one could try to 'watch him at work and observing what the word
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text suggests that conceptual meanings in mathematics are revealed by observing practices and operations, not solely by abstract philosophical definition.
